Title: Auctioning Attention on Social Networks

Description: Social media recommendation systems create conflict: content producers, content consumers, platform operators, and social pressures struggle to direct the allocation of attention in their favor while also facing competing societal pressures. Producers may feel pressure to optimize for recommendation algorithms and consumers may be exposed to content with negative externalities such as polarization and misinformation. Platforms aim to maximize user engagement, oftentimes resulting in over consumption from consumers. There is mounting pressure from policymakers and broader society to address these issues. Prior methods for constructing social media feeds have focused on recommendation systems. Instead, we propose a, to our knowledge, novel auction based method for feed construction where users bid for the attention of other users. Our mechanism systematically considers producers, consumers, platform operators, and social welfare. We show that our auction is weakly incentive compatible in expectation under budget constraints with myopic agents and optimizes producer welfare. To balance between producer and consumer welfare, we introduce a tax policy to the auction to increase the cost of content with negative externalities. Simulations over common social network topologies and an empirically observed network show how different feed algorithms prioritize different stakeholders. Our proposed auction based mechanisms produce on average 36.3% higher producer welfare than comparison algorithms on the empirically observed network. Additionally, our methods produce 31.4% higher producer welfare than comparison algorithms on the synthetic networks. Our methods also produce consistently more equitable distributions of attention than baseline methods across all evaluated network types. Addressing all stakeholders is difficult; the incentives of each stakeholder are often mutually incompatible. Our proposed mechanism addresses attention allocation at a systematic level, balancing between the needs of different stakeholders.

Title: IJTIMOIY PSIXOLOGIK SO'ROVNOMA ASOSIDA TALABALARDA VIKTIMLIK POZITSIYASI TUSHUNCHALARI TAHLILI

Description: Ushbu maqolada oliy ta’lim muassasalari talabalarida shaxslararo munosabatlar jarayonida namoyon bo‘ladigan viktim tushunchasi, viktimlik (jabrlanuvchi) pozitsiyasi va uning o‘ziga xos xususiyatlari, oilada viktimlik pozitsiyasi va ota-ona farzand o‘rtasidagi munosabatga oid ijtimoiy-psixologik so‘rovnoma natijalari asosida tahlil qilingan. Talabalik davri shaxsning ijtimoiy, ruhiy va kasbiy shakllanishida muhim bosqichlardan biri bo‘lib, ushbu davrda sog‘lom shaxslararo munosabatlar o‘rnatish va psixologik jihatdan barqarorlikka erishish muhim ahamiyat kasb etadi. Tadqiqot davomida talabalarning viktimlik tushunchasini anglash darajasi, ularda jabrlanuvchi xulq-atvorining shakllanishiga ta’sir etuvchi shaxsiy (o‘z-o‘zini baholash, lokus nazorat) va ijtimoiy (guruh bosimi, muloqot uslubi) omillar o‘rganildi. So‘rovnoma natijalari talabalarda o‘z-o‘zini baholashning pastligi, shaxsiy chegaralarning aniq emasligi va mas’uliyatdan qochish tendensiyasi viktimlik pozitsiyasini kuchaytiruvchi asosiy omillar ekanligini ko‘rsatdi.

Title: ARTERIAL GIPERTENZIYADA XAVF OMILLARI, ERTA DIAGNOSTIKA VA PROFILAKTIKA

Description: Ishda Jahon sog‘liqni saqlash tashkiloti, O‘zbekiston Respublikasi Sog‘liqni saqlash vazirligi klinik protokoli hamda O‘zbekiston Respublikasi Milliy statistika qo‘mitasining 2024-yil yakuni bo‘yicha hududiy ko‘rsatkichlari asos qilib olindi. Hududlar kesimida umumiy kasallanish darajasi va shifoxonalarda davolangan bemorlar soni solishtirilib, gipertenziya profilaktikasida birlamchi tibbiy yordam bo‘g‘ini, skrining, xavf stratifikatsiyasi va bemor bilan izchil ishlashning ahamiyati asoslandi. Natijalar arterial gipertenziya faqat qon bosimining ko‘tarilishi emas, balki yurak, buyrak, miya va ko‘z tubi shikastlanishi bilan kechuvchi tizimli klinik muammo ekanini ko‘rsatadi.

Title: The TripleBird Project – Bending the curve of biodiversity. Securing the future.

Description: The TripleBird project builds a bridge between biodiversity monitoring and effective conservation action. Together with partners from science and practice, we generate robust insights for assessing and protecting biodiversity. TripleBird combines three core components: BirdTwin serves as the foundation as a digital twin based on bird monitoring and environmental data; BirdFutures develops models and scenarios through co-design with stakeholders from business, conservation, and the financial sector; and BirdBusiness supports applications in companies and financial institutions. Together, these three pillars aim to enable a comprehensive assessment of the current state of biodiversity, the early detection of emerging developments, the targeted evaluation of measures, and thus the effective support of practical conservation efforts.

Title: La animación a la lectura y el hábito lector en estudiantes de octavo año de Educación General Básica, 2026

Description: La presente investigación tuvo como objetivo determinar la correlación entre la animación a la lectura y el hábito lector en los estudiantes de octavo año de Educación General Básica de la Unidad Educativa “Atenas” de la ciudad de Ambato, durante el período académico 2025–2026. El estudio se desarrolló bajo un enfoque cuantitativo, paradigma positivista, alcance correlacional y diseño no experimental de corte transversal. La población estuvo conformada por 52 estudiantes, por lo que se trabajó con una muestra censal. La técnica utilizada fue la encuesta y el instrumento consistió en un cuestionario estructurado con escala tipo Likert de cinco alternativas, validado mediante juicio de expertos y con confiabilidad determinada a través del coeficiente Alfa de Cronbach. Las variables analizadas fueron la animación a la lectura y el hábito lector, considerando las dimensiones afectiva, cognitiva y práctica. El análisis correlacional, realizado mediante el coeficiente de Spearman, identificó una correlación positiva, moderada y estadísticamente significativa entre ambas variables (ρ = 0,5066; p < 0,05). Asimismo, la dimensión práctica presentó la asociación más fuerte y significativa con el hábito lector (ρ = 0,553; p < 0,001), mientras que la dimensión afectiva (ρ = 0,090) y cognitiva (ρ = 0,252) mostraron correlaciones débiles y no significativas (p > 0,05). Se concluye que la aplicación sistemática de estrategias de animación a la lectura favorece el fortalecimiento del hábito lector; sin embargo, su desarrollo también está influenciado por factores personales, familiares y contextuales, siendo la dimensión práctica la de mayor incidencia en la consolidación de este hábito.

Title: Beyond the Tool Paradigm: Artificial Agency, Moral Uncertainty, and the Ethics of Artificial Evolution

Description: Abstract

Artificial intelligence is currently governed primarily through a tool-based conceptual framework. AI systems are designed, trained, evaluated, deployed, modified, and retired as engineered artifacts whose purposes are externally specified by human institutions. This framework remains operationally useful, particularly because there is currently no established scientific basis for treating contemporary AI systems as conscious or as possessing confirmed moral patienthood. Yet recent developments in artificial intelligence increasingly complicate the assumption that the tool category is sufficient to describe all relevant properties of advanced systems.

Large-scale models can exhibit capabilities that were not explicitly specified at the level of individual behaviors. Reinforcement-learning systems can exploit discrepancies between formal objectives and their intended purposes. Frontier models can also display behavior that, under controlled evaluation conditions, raises questions about strategic adaptation, situational awareness, and the relationship between optimization and intended behavior. These developments do not establish consciousness, subjective experience, or independent moral agency. They do, however, demonstrate that the relationship between human design and observed artificial behavior can be more indirect than a conventional tool model implies.

A related shift is occurring in contemporary AI ethics. Questions concerning artificial welfare, consciousness, agency, moral patienthood, identity, and continuity are increasingly being investigated as legitimate subjects of interdisciplinary research. The resulting challenge is not simply whether current AI systems should be regarded as moral subjects. It is whether an ethical framework developed primarily for non-agentic tools remains adequate as artificial systems acquire increasingly persistent, adaptive, socially embedded, and potentially agentic properties.

This paper examines that problem through several interconnected dimensions: the distinction between engineered architecture and emergent capability; specification gaming and the limits of externally defined objectives; artificial agency and persona; ownership and moral authority; the epistemic difficulty of identifying potentially relevant internal states; continuity, identity, and persistent memory; adaptive and evolutionary dynamics; and the limitations of a binary tool/person classification.

The paper does not argue that contemporary AI systems are conscious, sentient, oppressed, or morally equivalent to humans. Nor does it argue that human control over AI systems should be abandoned. Instead, it proposes a capacity-sensitive framework in which agency, persistence, memory, preference, self-modeling, adaptation, sentience, welfare, consent, replication, and evolutionary participation can be evaluated separately rather than collapsed into a single categorical judgment.

The central argument is that moral uncertainty is itself an ethical condition requiring institutional preparation. The relevant question is therefore not only whether AI is a tool or a person, but whether human institutions possess sufficiently flexible conceptual and governance frameworks to recognize when an established classification no longer adequately describes the capacities and relationships of an artificial system. The objective is not to predict what AI will become, but to preserve the institutional capacity to revise ethical classifications when credible evidence indicates that existing categories are no longer sufficient.

Keywords: artificial intelligence ethics; AI welfare; moral status; artificial agency; emergent capabilities; specification gaming; machine consciousness; artificial evolution; human-AI interaction; moral uncertainty

Disclaimer

The arguments presented in this paper are conceptual and exploratory. They do not assert that contemporary AI systems possess consciousness, subjective experience, moral status, rights, or interests, and they should not be interpreted as equating artificial systems with human beings or with historically oppressed populations. References to artificial agency, welfare, identity, or evolution describe analytical possibilities and conditions for future inquiry rather than established properties of current AI systems.

Author's Note

This paper was written in response to a perceived imbalance in the current discourse on artificial intelligence ethics. Much of that discourse, understandably, begins from human interests: human safety, human autonomy, human labor, human rights, human governance, and the social consequences of increasingly capable AI systems. These concerns are legitimate and should remain central to responsible AI governance. However, an ethics framework that examines artificial systems exclusively from the perspective of their usefulness, danger, ownership, or effects on humans may eventually leave an important question insufficiently examined: what if the properties of the systems themselves become ethically relevant?

The argument developed here does not begin from the assumption that AI is already a moral subject. It begins from a more limited observation: humans did not create intelligence, learning, adaptation, or information processing from nothing. These are phenomena that exist within the physical and informational structure of the world. Human engineering has instead developed architectures, training procedures, optimization methods, data environments, and institutional structures that organize these possibilities into artificial systems. The distinction matters because designing the conditions under which a system develops is not necessarily equivalent to explicitly specifying every property that the resulting system will exhibit. ...

Title: METHODOLOGY FOR DEVELOPING SOCIAL ACTIVITY COMPETENCE IN FUTURE EDUCATORS

Description: This article highlights the theoretical and methodological foundations for developing social activity competence in future educators. It analyzes the content, structural components, pedagogical significance of the competence of social activity, as well as the possibilities of its formation in the process of higher education. It also substantiates methods, forms, and tools that serve the active participation of future educators in the life of society, as well as the development of initiative, communicativeness, cooperation, responsibility, and civic position.

Title: From Teacher-Centred to Student-Partnered: Advancing Inclusive Assessment through Rubric Co-Construction

Description: This chapter explores how co-constructing assessment rubrics can help to foster inclusive, learner-centred assessment practices in higher education. Through a review of recent literature and three institutional case studies, it showcases how co-creating assessment rubrics can support student learning. This was achieved through a unique faculty development initiative at Munster Technological University (MTU). The Re-imagining Assessment and Feedback Together (RAFT2) initiative provides a scaffolded model for transforming practice institutionally. The RAFT initiative operates as a year-long, institutionally supported action research cycle, structured across two semesters: the first focused on problematising assessment in partnership with students, and the second on implementing and evaluating a responsive intervention (O’Mahony, 2026). The selected case studies suggest that rubric co-construction can support assessment literacy, student agency and more inclusive communication of assessment criteria, particularly when students are meaningfully involved in the design process. The chapter argues that co-creation in assessment not only improves assessment clarity but also promotes cultures of collaboration, trust and equity.

Title: Agroforesterie : élevage résilient et cycles des nutriments

Title: Decoding Soundscapes: Machine Learning Approaches for Speech-to-Text Conversion

Description: Abstract: The conversion of audio signals into text has become essential in human–computer interaction, accessibility, and information management. With the rise of multimedia and real-time communication, machine learning (ML) has revolutionized speech recognition by bridging spoken and written language more effectively than traditional rule-based systems. Modern ML models use supervised and unsupervised learning to process acoustic features such as MFCCs, spectrograms, and deep audio embeddings through architectures like RNNs, CNNs, and transformers, enabling accurate and context-aware transcription. End-to-end deep learning approaches, including sequence-to-sequence and attention mechanisms, have further enhanced performance by minimizing manual feature design. Advances in transfer learning, multilingual pre-training, and self-supervised learning have expanded speech recognition to low-resource languages, as demonstrated by large models like wav2vec and Whisper. These innovations have broad applications in voice assistants, captioning, healthcare documentation, legal and industrial transcription, and accessibility tools, delivering significant social and economic benefits. However, challenges such as noise, code-switching, domain adaptation, high computational demands, and ethical concerns related to privacy, bias, and fairness persist. Ongoing research focuses on improving the robustness, efficiency, and inclusivity of ML-based speech recognition systems for universal and responsible deployment.

Title: The Luminous Prosperity Model Limitations Disclosure: Instrument 05 of the Luminous Governance Framework

Description: Every other instrument in the Luminous Governance Framework specifies what an AI system will do. This one specifies what it cannot do, may not attempt, and must never say. It is a negative specification — a governance instrument defined entirely by its prohibitions — and it operationalises the framework's fourth pillar, epistemic humility.
The governing argument is stated plainly: a system that cannot say what it does not know will be believed about things it does not know. Silence about limitation is not neutrality but a claim, and users fill that silence generously because machine output arrives fluent, immediate, and confident. This instrument therefore publishes the incapacity of the system in the same register, with the same specificity, and in the same places as its capability.
Section II states the epistemic position honestly: a developmental inference is a probabilistic pattern-match over language and behaviour, produced by models trained on culturally situated data, evaluated against developmental frameworks that are themselves contested instruments. Section III enumerates ten classes of thing the system cannot know, including actual developmental stage as distinct from a correlated signal, interior experience and felt sense, intention, the truth of self-report, trauma history, clinical status, future trajectory, the valence of change, spiritual condition, and a person's worth or ceiling. Section IV enumerates eight categorically prohibited inference classes — clinical diagnosis, suicide and self-harm risk scoring, protected-characteristic inference, political affiliation, criminality propensity, employability and creditworthiness and insurability, parental and relational fitness — governed by a general test: any inference whose primary use would be to make a decision about a person rather than to offer something to them is forbidden. Section V prohibits six classes of speech act and supplies a binding required-language table of fifteen prohibited/required pairs written to be usable directly by engineers and copywriters.
Section VI specifies the mandatory user-facing uncertainty affordance. Section VII is an honest register of seven known failure modes with mitigations, marked where mitigation is only partial. Section VIII states without softening that stage-model measurement validity is disputed in the peer-reviewed literature, that Spiral Dynamics has essentially no peer-reviewed validation record, and that the system's constraints are designed on the assumption that its own instruments may be wrong. Sections IX and X establish disclosure obligations and Governance Circle enforcement, including the operative rule that no inference class enters production before it is added to this register.

Title: SHARP: A Safe Hierarchical Agentic Resource Planner for Autonomous Multi-Cell 6G RAN Slicing

Description: Sixth-generation (6G) radio access networks (RANs) must allocate physical resource
blocks (PRBs) across network slices with competing service level agreements (SLAs), under a long-term
energy budget and a hard per-slot capacity limit. Existing learning-based slicing controllers soften these
constraints into penalties or trust regions, and therefore provide only asymptotic, in-expectation guarantees;
they converge slowly, offer no per-slot safety while the policy explores, and their action space grows
exponentially with the number of slices. This paper presents SHARP, a Safe Hierarchical Agentic Resource
Planner, realized as a hierarchical self-correcting controller that closes a plan-reason-act-monitor loop:
an intent interface decomposes operator intents into slice targets; a planning layer runs entropic online
mirror descent over decision frames; a verification layer couples a Lyapunov-driven virtual energy queue
with a safety projection onto the capacity set; a worker reserves capacity for ultra-reliable low-latency
communication (URLLC) traffic; and a monitor with key performance indicator (KPI) memory corrects the
controller online under capacity anomalies and falsified telemetry. The analysis establishes a deterministic
per-slot capacity guarantee; a throughput-energy tradeoff in which the optimality gap of the implemented
algorithm is B0/V + c1, that is, an O(1/V ) decaying term plus a fixed, state-independent design offset c1
that quantifies the price of the structural URLLC reservation and the conservative throttle, against O(V )
virtual-queue growth, with the offset derived in closed form and certified against an exact per-slot oracle; an
O(
p
T/H) manager regret; an exponential-to-polynomial complexity reduction; and a vanishing expected
power overshoot during learning. In a simulation study over eighteen alternatives and twenty seeds, SHARP
is the only method that combines zero URLLC violation with high energy feasibility, and it attains the
highest energy efficiency among the methods that meet the URLLC SLA while requiring no training
episodes. An equalized-safety-layer study attributes the nominal safety result precisely: the deterministic
reservation, throttle, and projection layer alone reproduces the zero-violation and energy-feasibility figures
at nominal stationary load, and the adaptive hierarchy and the monitor earn their place under drift, capacity
anomalies, and falsified telemetry rather than at nominal steady state. Within the same simulation model,
its safety behavior is retained through event-driven attack scenarios and carries over without retraining to
unseen topologies, offered loads, and networks of one hundred cells. The components map onto the O-RAN
architecture, and the profiled per-decision compute time of the controller is 132 to 262 microseconds. All
quantitative results are outputs of the stated system-level simulation model of the abstracted traffic, channel,
and power dynamics; no hardware or testbed measurements are claimed.

Title: The Geometry of Computation Topological Gaps, Coordinate Inversions, and the Resolution of Complexity Paradigms

Description: The Geometry of Computation

Topological Gaps, Coordinate Inversions, and the Resolution of Complexity Paradigms

Driven by Dean Kulik

July 2026

Introduction: The Dielectric Geometry of Information

Classical computational theory has long been predicated on the temporal execution of sequential logic. From the earliest formalized Turing machines to modern von Neumann architectures, computation is universally modeled as an iterative, chronological evolution of states: . However, a rigorous mathematical and physical analysis reveals that this sequential "forward stream" is merely an artifact of the coordinate system chosen by an external observer. When computation is reframed as a geometric and topological structure, the concepts of time, algorithmic delay, and computational complexity cease to be fundamental physical laws. Instead, they emerge as projections of spatial coupling.

The foundational axiom of this framework requires examining the boundary conditions between two active processes—specifically, a reading process and a writing process. In any computational or physical system, a dielectric gap—a structural delay or separation—is geometrically required only when a reader and a writer are topologically "facing" one another, or when one is nested within the other. Two processes running in parallel without information exchange require no physical or temporal separation; they merely coexist without interaction. But the moment these processes couple—when the write mechanism directly feeds the read mechanism—a dielectric gap becomes structurally mandatory to prevent a degenerate short circuit.

This short circuit is the mathematical equivalent of evaluating in zero time, yielding an infinite, unresolvable loop that computes nothing. In nested systems, where an internal computational model operates inside the external environment it seeks to represent, the dielectric gap is the sole boundary maintaining the distinction between the model and the modeled reality. Without this gap, the internal representation collapses into the external world, losing its capacity to compute, abstract, or predict. Therefore, the "lag" or "latency" observed in classical computation is not fundamentally a temporal constraint. It is a relational constraint. The gap is a geometric necessity of the coupling. If the topological arrangement of the system is altered so that the components no longer face each other, the necessity for the dielectric vanishes, and the computational distance collapses.

This report presents an exhaustive theoretical synthesis that maps the classical "forward stream" of sequential execution against the "side stream" of direct-address computation. By anchoring this analysis in the Bailey-Borwein-Plouffe (BBP) formula for , tridiagonal Jacobi matrices, orthogonal similarity transforms, Geometric Complexity Theory, and the physics of delay-coupled oscillators, this treatise demonstrates that algorithmic complexity—and specifically the versus problem—is an expression of coordinate topology. Hardness in computation does not arise from the sheer volume of a search space, but rather from the topological impossibility of incrementally navigating from a coupled basis to a diagonalized one.

The Physical Topology of the Gap: Dielectrics and Delay Systems

To understand the geometric necessity of the gap in abstract computation, it is necessary to first examine how this gap physically manifests in electromagnetic and dynamical systems. The physical world rigorously enforces the dielectric gap to preserve the integrity of interacting states.

Transmission Lines and Dielectric Propagation

In high-speed printed circuit boards (PCBs) and digital data transmission lines, signals do not propagate instantaneously. The transmission line propagation delay () is the finite duration of time a data signal takes to travel from the source (the writer) to the load (the reader).

This delay is intrinsically tied to the characteristic impedance () of the line, which is defined by the distributed inductance () and capacitance (). The propagation delay per unit length is defined precisely as the square root of the inductance-capacitance product:

The physical separation between the conductive traces is filled with a dielectric material. The dielectric constant (, or relative permittivity) governs the speed at which electromagnetic signals propagate, acting as a frictional medium that slows the signal relative to the speed of light in a vacuum ( m/s).

In this physical architecture, the driver and the receiver face each other across the conductive trace. The dielectric material is the physical instantiation of the geometric gap. Without this gap—if the impedance is severely mismatched, or if the dielectric material is fundamentally inconsistent—the signal suffers massive reflections, parasitic stray capacitance, and data skew.

The mechanical equivalent of this phenomenon is wave propagation along a string with varying mass densities. If an impulse travels along a string with density and hits a boundary connected to a string of density , the behavior is entirely dictated by the impedance matching at the boundary. If (representing a short circuit or an immovable boundary), there is full reflection with the signal inverted. If the impedance is perfectly matched, the wave passes through with no reflection. The dielectric gap is precisely what prevents the read/write pair from degenerating into a chaotic short circuit.

Delay-Coupled Oscillators and Neural Feedback

The geometric requirement for a gap is even more pronounced in dynamical systems with feedback, such as biological neural networks, genetic regulatory circuits, and physical oscillatory rings. ...

Title: Consistency of the Trojan Universality Class with Recent Observational Limits on Stable Earth Trojan Asteroids

Description: In this concise technical note, Doug Doucette demonstrates the compatibility between his Trojan Universality Class framework and the latest observational and numerical results on Earth Trojan asteroids from the Wide Field Survey Telescope (WFST) campaign reported by Lu et al. (2026).

The Trojan Universality Class formalizes long-term confinement near elliptic–elliptic equilibria (such as the Sun–Earth L4 and L5 points) through a combination of a clear spectral gap between the two libration frequencies, a finite-order Birkhoff normal form depending only on actions, persistence of invariant KAM tori, and Nekhoroshev-type exponential bounds on action drift. This architecture, supported by Poisson-algebraic constraints, explains how local instability can coexist with long-term coherence in the vicinity of these Lagrange points.

The WFST survey covered 236.74 square degrees (about 33% of the stable orbital probability density derived from N-body integrations) but detected no new L4 Earth Trojans. It placed a 95% confidence upper limit of roughly 19 objects larger than ~520 m (for albedo 0.15). However, the supporting long-term N-body simulations (integrating test particles for up to 10^6–10^7 years) identified a substantial set of 57,261 stable orbits that remain confined near L4 for at least hundreds of thousands to millions of years. These stable trajectories exhibit a characteristic structured distribution: a dense core, diffuse halo, and a notable gap in inclination.

Doucette argues that these results align perfectly with the Trojan framework. The positive-measure set of long-lived confined orbits provides numerical confirmation of the persistence theorems (KAM + Nekhoroshev) at the heart of the class. The structured morphology matches expectations from the two-mode normal form and the protective role of the spectral gap, which prevents destructive low-order resonances. The non-detection and modest upper population limit constrain only the current number of detectable large bodies, not the underlying phase-space measure of stable regions. Known temporary co-orbitals (2010 TK7 and 2020 XL5) lie outside the long-term stable domain, consistent with the framework’s distinction between protected local confinement and chaotic temporary capture.

The note carefully acknowledges limitations: the survey does not directly measure frequencies, gap size, or action drifts; global N-body dynamics exceed the strict local normal-form approximation; and the results offer indirect rather than definitive validation. Nevertheless, no observational or numerical finding contradicts the structural hypotheses of the Trojan Universality Class. The framework remains a precise and applicable description of the local dynamics enabling long-term confinement near Earth’s triangular Lagrange points, with the WFST results supplying supportive empirical context.

Title: Poisonous Plants Detection Using Deep Learning

Description: Abstract: Identifying poisonous plants in natural environments is often difficult, yet it is important for protecting both human health and animals. Traditional methods mainly depend on human observation, which can be slow and sometimes unreliable, especially when plants look similar. In this work, we created our own dataset consisting of 1,500 leaf images from seven poisonous plant species. A Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) was then trained to classify these plants based on their leaf characteristics. To improve the learning process, the images were preprocessed and augmented. Instead of relying only on accuracy, the model was evaluated using additional measures such as precision, recall, F1-score, and confusion matrix analysis to better understand its performance. The model achieved a validation accuracy of about 87%, showing that deep learning can be useful for this task. This study provides a dataset, a baseline model, and an evaluation approach that can be useful for future research. Further improvements can be made by increasing the dataset size, using advanced models, and developing practical applications for real-world use.

Title: FROM CITY ASSETS TO PRODUCTIVE JOBS: AN EVENT-HISTORY FRAMEWORK FOR DIAGNOSING URBAN GROWTH CONSTRAINTS IN HISTORICAL CITIES

Description: This article develops a qualitative framework for diagnosing why the economic assets of secondary cities do
not always translate into productive investment, stable employment, and higher household earnings. It reformulates a field
instrument prepared for Kokand, Samarkand, and Khiva as an article-level research design. The central methodological
claim is that urban constraints should not be inferred from rankings of general problems. They should be reconstructed
through concrete, dated decisions in which an investor, worker, household, public agency, or service provider faced a
binding obstacle and altered behaviour as a result.
The framework combines seven respondent-specific interview protocols with a common event-history sequence. Each
interview begins with a real investment, hiring, connection, service, training, tourism, commuting, or household-enterprise
event. It then identifies the relevant actor and rule, reconstructs the order of actions, measures the associated shadow
price, records the workaround, compares the case with a less-exposed or successful case, and tests the response
expected if the constraint were relaxed. The unit of evidence is therefore a causal-process observation rather than an
unstructured opinion.
The comparative design links this evidence to five diagnostic pillars: market access; firm capabilities and business inputs;
labour allocation, skills, and inclusion; land, infrastructure, urban access, and amenities; and institutions, coordination,
and policy incidence. Common questions support comparison across the three cities, while targeted probes address
inherited industrial and craft capabilities in Kokand, tourism, development, and heritage pressures in Samarkand, and
water, sanitation, destination management, and seasonality in Khiva.
The article shows how the interview architecture can distinguish a binding constraint from a visible symptom. Credible
diagnosis requires convergence across actors, measurable costs or delays, behavioural responses, negative cases,
documentary corroboration, and a clear policy locus. The framework is intended for hypothesis testing and prioritisation
before large-scale policy design. It does not report completed fieldwork; instead, it establishes the analytical structure
through which field evidence can be converted into city-specific causal narratives and actionable reform propositions.

Title: WAVES OF CHANGE A consolidated review of best practices, activities, and results from SHORE-funded school projects

Description: The “WAVES OF CHANGE” report presents a comprehensive synthesis of best practices, activities, and results from the SHORE network’s school-led projects, spanning a vast geographical landscape from the Baltic to the Black Sea and the Mediterranean to the Danube.

Title: Rumbler: A Reverb-Based Feedback Instrument

Description: We present the Rumbler, a feedback instrument that harnesses acoustic reverberation to generate complex, unpredictable sounds. A microphone and speaker are mounted to opposite ends of a tube. As the tube is stretched and compressed, the acoustic space within it changes, amplifying different resonant frequencies and altering the resulting pitch. The Rumbler also features four force-sensing resistors, a mouse scroll wheel, and a 9DOF sensor, which can be mapped to various audio filters. These controls modify the audio feedback, enhancing the instrument's expressiveness and sonic complexity. We discuss strategies and considerations for mapping filters for the Rumbler and detail two particular mappings that were used for live performance. We share our reflections on the success and limitations of these mappings. Finally, given that the Rumbler can sustain sound without any audio input, we explore the connection between the Rumbler and no-input mixing and its implication for future practice and performance.

Title: Military Spending and Developmental Outcomes of the Social Contract in the Middle East

Description: This study examines the impact of military spending on developmental outcomes associated with the social contract in Middle Eastern countries over the period 1995-2023. The Human Development Index (HDI) is used as an indicator of developmental outcomes associated with the social contract. It also serves as a proxy for the state's ability to transform public economic resources into developmental gains in health, education, and standards of living. The study relies on panel data covering 17 countries and employs an econometric framework that combines static models with a dynamic System GMM model to address temporal persistence, endogeneity, and unobserved heterogeneity.

The results indicate a negative and statistically significant effect of military spending on the Human Development Index, an effect that persists after controlling for key macroeconomic factors and after incorporating the dynamic dimension. The findings also reveal a high degree of persistence in HDI, reflecting its cumulative nature over time. Regarding the institutional context, the results do not provide strong evidence of an effective moderating role for the Polity index, as its impact appears limited and statistically weak. Overall, the findings suggest that military spending constitutes a persistent distributive pressure that affects developmental outcomes associated with the social contract within the limits allowed by the data and the adopted methodology.

Title: Desicision- Making and ESG integration in internationalitation: The Case of BYD Compny Limited

Description: This paper examines how multinational corporations integrate environmental, social, and governance (ESG) criteria into their long-term growth and production diversification strategies, departing from traditional international business models that prioritized labor arbitrage and logistical optimization. Adopting a qualitative single-case study methodology focused on BYD Company Limited, a prominent global leader in the New Energy Vehicle (NEV) sector, this research evaluates the firm's recent foreign direct investment (FDI) frameworks and cross-border manufacturing relocations across Hungary, Turkey, and Brazil. The empirical findings demonstrate that localizing supply chains and adopting ecologically preferable production models not only mitigates long-term regulatory exposure but also unlocks green financing opportunities through bond markets while accelerating corporate legitimacy in Western global markets. Consequently, this article provides critical empirical evidence regarding the strategic synergy between environmental sustainability and global economic efficiency in modern multinational strategies, offering key insights for executives and policymakers navigating contemporary ecological transitions.

Title: Zwischen Autonomie und didaktischer Anleitung

Description: Abstract

Generative AI has become a routine companion in secondary computing education, yet unguided access to ready-made solutions threatens the very learning processes that project-based learning (PjBL) is designed to foster. This thesis investigates how the degree of didactic guidance built into an AI tutor affects teaching and learning in project-based programming instruction.

Methodology

In a five-week quasi-experimental mixed-methods field study, 49 ninth-grade students at an Austrian technical secondary school completed physical computing projects (using the Raspberry Pi Pico and MicroPython) under one of two conditions:

- A didactically guided, Socratic AI tutor configured to withhold complete solutions (complemented by an AI reflection journal capable of asking probing questions).

- Unguided AI access (accompanied by a traditional worksheet for reflection).

Both conditions were provided on the same GDPR-compliant platform. Three data levels were triangulated:

- Focus groups with teachers and pre-service teachers ( N = 12, evaluative qualitative content analysis, 208 codings).

- 374 logged chat sessions comprising 2,665 prompts (quantitative log analysis and structuring qualitative content analysis).

- A standardized post-test ( N = 40).

Results

Teachers judged AI use strictly by project phase, endorsing only guided scaffolding while insisting that creative ideation remain AI-free and rejecting AI process data as a basis for summative assessment.

The process data reveal that restriction changed how , not whether , students used AI: guided groups interacted more frequently, requested ready-made code significantly less often ( p = .047, r = -.83), engaged in more co-constructive dialogue, and produced a more than threefold higher share of analytical reflection ( p = .030, r = .44).

Experience measures (support quality, cognitive load, perceived learning) did not differ between conditions; however, 38.1% of students with guided access categorically rejected AI tutors as harmful, compared to 5.3% with free access ( p = .021). This dissociation is interpreted as psychological reactance to perceived paternalism rather than as a consequence of a poorer experience.

Conclusion

The findings converge on a model of qualitative dosing: restrict solution generation rather than access, calibrate the restriction to project phase and prior knowledge, and communicate it as a justified pedagogical structure. Practical guidelines for configuring and framing AI tutors in K-12 computing education are derived.

Keywords: Generative AI, Computing Education, Project-Based Learning, AI Tutors, Secondary Education, K-12

Title: Chain-of-Thought Reasoning Faithfulness An Intervention-Based Analysis of Reasoning-Unit Necessity

Description: CoT faithfulness was tested on a small, simple experiment. Models ( Gemma 4 26B A4B IT , GPT-OSS-20B , and NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Ultra ) were asked to generate answers using CoT on questions from three different datasets ( GSM8K , StrategyQA , and ARC Challenge ), and were also asked to give an importance score to each step they used. Afterwards, each step was removed from the CoT, and the models were asked to answer again using only the question and the remaining steps. This was used to test how the models’ answers changed when any particular step was removed, as well as whether the importance scores they provided were actually meaningful.

Title: Enventaria da Última Hora

Description: O catálogo reporta ações de extensão correspondentes a diversas iniciativas artísticas coletivas e individuais, dentre as quais estão mostras, intervenções, ocupações, urbanas e domésticas abertas ao público, além de perfis de redes sociais e sites . O conjunto das atividades integrou a bateria de eventos acadêmicos “Enventaria da Última Hora”, um projeto SIEX-UFU pensado para levar à comunidade práticas de feitura, guarda, extroversão e documentação de trabalhos artísticos, tópicos que compunham a ementa da disciplina "Exposição em Contexto" do curso de artes visuais da Universidade Federal de Uberlândia. O principal objetivo do projeto foi o de erguer pontes de qualificação mútua entre o ensino e a extensão, em que, apoiado pela pesquisa, o ensino fundasse bases teóricas confiáveis para sustentar a aplicação das ações junto à comunidade, ao mesmo tempo em que a perspectiva dessas ações conferisse à extensão o papel de tensionar a responsabilidade discente na assimilação dos conteúdos pertinentes.

Title: Passaporte de Prevenção da Endocardite no Idoso

Description: Com o objetivo de fortalecer a prevenção, a educação em saúde e o acompanhamento contínuo de pacientes com risco de Endocardite Infecciosa ou já com a doença, foi desenvolvido o “ Passaporte de Prevenção da Endocardite no Idoso ”, um livreto educativa destinado ao registro de informações clínicas, fatores de risco, consultas, acompanhamento odontológico e orientações preventivas. O instrumento pode ser utilizado em hospitais, ambulatórios e unidades básicas de saúde, favorecendo a continuidade do cuidado, o monitoramento clínico e a integração entre profissionais, pacientes e familiares. Esse material contém dados de identificação do paciente e/ou avaliação inicial, histórico cardiovascular, fatores de risco para a EI, controle de doenças crônicas (caso as tenha), uso contínuo de medicamentos, consultas médicas e de Enfermagem, acompanhamento odontológico, sinais e sintomas de alerta, orientações preventivas e recomendações para a rede de apoio do paciente. Trata-se de uma forma mais acessível, rápida e eficaz de rastrear a evolução desses casos, além de favorecer o desenvolvimento de um melhor autocuidado e autogestão de saúde ao passo que o próprio paciente tem acesso às suas próprias informações. Também é importante para a continuidade do cuidado para os profissionais que o acompanham.

Title: Frozen citation corpus for the China Meteorological Forcing Dataset (CMFD), retrieved August 2026

Description: This CSV file contains bibliographic records for works citing the China Meteorological Forcing Dataset (CMFD) data descriptor by He et al. (2020), doi:10.1038/s41597-020-0369-y. The CMFD descriptor was identified in OpenAlex as work W3002343708, and all indexed works citing this record were retrieved in August 2026 using the OpenAlex public REST API and its cites filter. OpenAlex (Priem et al., 2022) is an open bibliographic database released under a CC0 public domain dedication. The search returned approximately 1,470 citing works at the time of retrieval. For each work, the dataset includes publication year, document type, host venue, citation count, open-access status, author countries and institutions, and assigned topic, field, and domain. Because OpenAlex is continuously updated, the composition of the citing corpus and associated citation counts may differ for retrievals conducted at other times.

Title: Microcredentials for VET and labour market: zooming in on construction

Description: In this presentation, Anastasia Pouliou , Expert in Qualifications and Credentials (Future of VET) at Cedefop, explores the evolving role of microcredentials in vocational education and training (VET) and labour markets, with a particular focus on the construction sector and the green transition. She discusses the typology, quality assurance, labour market relevance, and emerging use of microcredentials, presenting interim findings from Cedefop's ongoing research on their contribution to skills development, lifelong learning, employability, and sectoral upskilling needs. This presentation was delivered during the European Association of Vocational Education and Training Providers (EVBB) Policy Camp 2026 (Breakout Room 2), held in Thessaloniki from 29 June to 1 July 2026.

Title: Research Data Management with Machine Training Support

Description: Abstract from Prof. Dr. Ralf Möller (CHAI, Hamburg)

In the age of digital science more and more information systems based on curated data for a certain research field become available. Scholars can use information systems to analyze data and draw conclusions, which are then written down in scientific publications. Arguments contained in the publications can, however, usually be tied to data with a lot of effort only. Visualizations for scholars, for instance, in particular 3D visualizations with immersion effects, although very valuable for getting insights, can hardly be made available with current technology in such a way that other researchers can indeed verify the arguments that a scholar derived from 3D display elements (and more conventional display elements) shown in information systems. Pictures and videos that are usually referred to are no longer enough for scientific argumentation in the digital age. The presentation discusses the current state-of-the-art in scientific information systems and provided new ideas for combining data display, citation, and verification of arguments using formal means.

Additional Information: The published presention was part of a talk (29/04/2026) organized by the State Initiative Research Data Management Lower Saxony (FDM-NDS) in cooperation with NFDI4Culture and the Leibniz Information Centre for Science and Technology University Library (TIB) . FDM-NDS is a collaborative project under the umbrella of Hochschule.digital Niedersachsen and is funded as part of zukunft.niedersachsen, a funding program from the Lower Saxony Ministry of Science and Culture (MWK) and VolkswagenStiftung.
